lessonTitle: MRI and Ultrasound: Contrast, Planes and Safety

blocks.text: A trauma team sweeps a handheld probe across a collapsed patient's abdomen and sees a black stripe of fluid between the liver and the kidney within a minute, at the bedside, with no radiation. In the next bay, a patient with a cardiac pacemaker is turned away from a magnet scanner that would otherwise have given the sharpest soft-tissue pictures in the hospital.

blocks.markdown: **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)** places the patient in a strong static magnetic field, commonly 1.5 or 3 tesla. Hydrogen nuclei (protons), mostly in water and fat, align with the field. A radiofrequency pulse tips them, and as they relax they emit signals that the scanner detects. MRI uses **no ionising radiation**. The signal depends on how quickly protons relax, which differs among tissues, so MRI shows excellent soft-tissue contrast.

blocks.title: T1 and T2 weighting
blocks.text: Weighting is the choice of timing parameters that emphasises one of the two relaxation processes. **T1-weighted** images show anatomy well, with fat bright and fluid dark. **T2-weighted** images emphasise water, with fluid bright and pathology such as oedema often bright.

blocks.caption: Approximate appearance of tissues on common spin-echo sequences; blood and special sequences vary.

blocks.title: Which sequence is this?
blocks.prompt: A brain image shows bright scalp fat and dark CSF in the ventricles. Is it T1- or T2-weighted, and what would you expect for CSF on the other sequence?

steps.text: Identify the fluid appearance: CSF in the ventricles is dark.
Identify fat: the scalp fat is bright.
Dark fluid with bright fat is the pattern of T1 weighting.
On a T2-weighted image of the same slice, CSF would be bright.

blocks.answer: T1-weighted; CSF would appear bright on T2.

blocks.markdown: MRI can produce images directly in any plane: **axial** (transverse, dividing top from bottom), **sagittal** (dividing left from right) and **coronal** (dividing front from back). A midsagittal plane passes through the midline, whereas a parasagittal plane is parallel to it at a distance from the midline. Spine imaging is typically sagittal and axial, and brain imaging usually uses all three planes.

**Ultrasound** uses sound at frequencies above human hearing, typically 2 to 15 MHz in medical imaging. A transducer sends short pulses into the body and detects echoes returned from interfaces between tissues of different **acoustic impedance**. The time taken for the echo to return gives the depth. Fluid-filled structures such as the bladder and cysts appear black (anechoic) because few echoes are returned from within. Bone and gas reflect nearly all sound, so they produce bright surfaces with a dark shadow behind them. The wavelength is $\lambda = c/f$, where $f$ is the frequency and $c$ the speed of sound, so higher frequencies have shorter wavelengths, give finer detail, but penetrate less.

blocks.caption: Depth $d$ of a reflector from the echo delay $t$, where $c \approx 1540\ \text{m/s}$ is the speed of sound in soft tissue; the factor of 2 accounts for the round trip.

blocks.title: Depth from echo time
blocks.prompt: An echo returns after $65\ \mu\text{s}$. Using $c = 1540\ \text{m/s}$, how deep is the reflector?

steps.text: The pulse travels to the reflector and back, so the depth is half the total path.
Convert the time to seconds: $65\ \mu\text{s} = 65\times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}$ and substitute.

rows: Good for superficial and fluid-filled structures
Ultrasound limited by bone and gas
Metal and implants in the magnet
blocks.caption: Comparing MRI and ultrasound.

blocks.markdown: **MRI safety.** The magnet is always on, so any ferromagnetic object becomes a projectile. Absolute or relative exclusions include cardiac pacemakers and defibrillators that are not MR-conditional, cochlear implants, older ferromagnetic intracranial aneurysm clips, metallic foreign bodies in the eye, and some neurostimulators. Radiofrequency energy can heat metal and cause burns. Other considerations are claustrophobia, loud noise, and caution in pregnancy (MRI is generally avoided early unless clearly needed). Gadolinium contrast needs care in severe renal impairment. Patients are screened with a checklist, and implants are checked against manufacturer data.

items: Screen every patient and visitor for implants, pacemakers, clips and metal fragments.
Remove all ferromagnetic objects before entering the scanner room.
Check whether an implant is MR-safe or MR-conditional.
Consider alternatives such as CT or ultrasound if MRI is unsafe.

blocks.title: Ultrasound at the bedside
blocks.text: Ultrasound is portable, quick, repeatable, free of ionising radiation and shows real-time movement and blood flow, so it is used for urgent assessment, pregnancy and guiding needles.

blocks.title: Never take metal into the MR room
blocks.text: Projectile injuries and burns have occurred when screening was incomplete. A pacemaker or cochlear implant that is not confirmed MR-conditional is a reason not to scan.

points: T1: fat bright and fluid dark. T2: fluid bright; fat bright on common fast spin-echo sequences.
Ultrasound uses reflected sound; depth = ct/2; fluid is black and bone or gas blocks the beam; it is portable and radiation-free.
MRI is excluded or restricted by non-conditional pacemakers, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic clips and orbital metal.

questions.stem: A sagittal MRI of the lumbar spine shows the intervertebral discs with bright signal and the CSF around the cauda equina bright. Which sequence is this most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bright CSF is the hallmark of T2 weighting.
distractorRationale.c: CT is not an MRI sequence.
distractorRationale.d: A radiograph is not an MRI sequence.

questions.explanation: CSF is fluid and appears bright on T2-weighted images, which emphasise water. On T1, CSF appears dark and fat is bright.

questions.stem: On a T1-weighted image of the knee, what appearance would you expect from a joint effusion and from the subcutaneous fat?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: on T1, fluid is dark and fat is bright.
distractorRationale.b: This is the reverse of the pattern.

questions.explanation: The T1 pattern is dark fluid and bright fat. A T2 image would show the effusion as bright.

questions.stem: A radiologist wants to demonstrate oedema in the spinal cord. Which sequence is most appropriate, and why?

options.text: T2-weighted, because water-rich tissue is bright
Plain radiograph, because oedema is dense
CT with contrast, because oedema is dark

questions.correctOptionText: T2-weighted, because water-rich tissue is bright

distractorRationale.a: Correct: T2 emphasises water so oedema is bright.
distractorRationale.b: Water is not bright on T1.
distractorRationale.c: Oedema is not seen on plain radiographs.
distractorRationale.d: CT is not the sequence referred to and does not show it well.

questions.explanation: T2-weighted sequences are sensitive to increased water content, so oedema stands out as a bright area. T1 sequences show anatomy with bright fat.

questions.stem: A returning echo is detected $130\ \mu\text{s}$ after the pulse. With $c = 1540\ \text{m/s}$ in soft tissue, calculate the depth of the reflector in cm using $d = ct/2$.
questions.explanation: d = 1540 x 130 x 10^-6 / 2 = 0.1001 m, which is about 10.0 cm. The division by 2 allows for the pulse travelling to the reflector and back.

questions.stem: An ultrasound transducer operates at 5 MHz. Using $c = 1540\ \text{m/s}$ and $\lambda = c/f$, calculate the wavelength in mm.
questions.explanation: λ = 1540 / (5 x 10^6) = 3.08 x 10^-4 m = 0.308 mm, about 0.31 mm. Shorter wavelengths give finer detail but are attenuated more, so they penetrate less.

questions.stem: A paramedic asks why ultrasound is used at the bedside in an unstable patient. Which is the best answer?

options.text: It is portable, real-time and uses no ionising radiation
It gives the best bone detail
It is unaffected by gas in bowel

questions.correctOptionText: It is portable, real-time and uses no ionising radiation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: portability, real-time imaging and no ionising radiation are advantages.
distractorRationale.b: Bone reflects sound, so detail is limited.
distractorRationale.c: Gas blocks ultrasound, so bowel gas is a limitation.
distractorRationale.d: Magnets are used in MRI, not ultrasound.

questions.explanation: Ultrasound machines are small and give instant images, which suits urgent assessment. Gas and bone limit what it can show.

questions.stem: In an ultrasound image of the bladder in a 40-year-old woman, the bladder lumen appears:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fluid returns almost no echoes and appears black.
distractorRationale.b: Bright white would suggest bone or calcification.
distractorRationale.d: A bright surface with shadow suggests bone or gas.

questions.explanation: Urine is a homogeneous fluid with no internal interfaces, so it is anechoic. The back wall often looks brighter because sound passes through fluid easily.

questions.stem: Which patient should NOT undergo MRI without further checking of device compatibility?

options.text: A patient with a cardiac pacemaker not known to be MR-conditional
A patient with a titanium dental filling
A patient wearing a cotton gown
A patient with an old bone plate that is known to be MR-conditional

questions.correctOptionText: A patient with a cardiac pacemaker not known to be MR-conditional

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a pacemaker not known to be MR-conditional is a key exclusion.
distractorRationale.b: Dental fillings are usually not a contraindication, though they may cause image artefact.
distractorRationale.d: An MR-conditional implant can be scanned under stated conditions.

questions.explanation: The magnet and radiofrequency fields can disrupt or heat a pacemaker's leads. Implants are scanned only when confirmed MR-conditional.

questions.stem: Explain why MRI is contraindicated in patients with older ferromagnetic intracranial aneurysm clips and with metal fragments in the eye. State two further safety considerations.
markingGuide: The strong static field can move ferromagnetic objects.
Movement or torque may injure vessels or ocular tissue.
Further: pacemaker or cochlear implant, claustrophobia, noise, pregnancy caution, gadolinium and renal function (any two).
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic objects experience forces and torque in the magnet, and in the brain or eye even a small movement can be catastrophic. Other hazards include heating and device malfunction.

questions.stem: Compare T1- and T2-weighted images in terms of the appearance of fat and fluid, and name one clinical situation where each is useful.
markingGuide: T2: fluid bright, fat intermediate to bright.
T1 shows anatomical detail, for example marrow or fat planes.
T2 shows oedema, effusions and many lesions.
questions.explanation: The weighting determines which tissue property dominates image contrast. T1 images are good for anatomy while T2 images are sensitive to pathology that increases water content.
